question: The main difference between a typical and an atypical antipsychotic drug is that an atypical drug:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors and causes fewer extrapyramidal effects

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Atypical drugs such as risperidone, olanzapine and clozapine block both dopamine and serotonin receptors and produce fewer extrapyramidal effects

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — has no effect on psychotic symptoms: All antipsychotics reduce psychotic symptoms

B — acts only on dopamine receptors and causes more extrapyramidal effects: Blocking only dopamine with marked extrapyramidal effects describes the typical drugs such as haloperidol

C — is given only by injection: Atypicals are available as oral and depot preparations

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Atypicals are preferred for long term use because the burden of movement side effects is lower, which improves adherence
option_2: acts only on dopamine receptors and causes more extrapyramidal effects
option_4: blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors and causes fewer extrapyramidal effects

question: Spasm of the neck muscles with the head twisted to one side, occurring within hours of an antipsychotic injection, is:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. acute dystonia

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Acute dystonia is a sustained muscle spasm of the neck, eyes or jaw that appears within hours to days of starting or increasing an antipsychotic

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — akathisia: Akathisia is an inner feeling of restlessness with inability to sit still

B — neuroleptic malignant syndrome: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare reaction with rigidity, fever and autonomic instability

C — tardive dyskinesia: Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect with involuntary movements of the face and tongue

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: A dystonic reaction is frightening for the patient, so reassurance is given along with the prescribed anticholinergic drug

question: A 24-year-old man received an injection of haloperidol six hours ago and now has a fixed twisting of the neck, difficulty in swallowing and severe distress. The nurse should first:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. stay with him, keep the airway safe, and give the prescribed intramuscular promethazine without delay

🧠 Clinical Rationale: An acute dystonic reaction with difficulty in swallowing needs prompt anticholinergic treatment such as promethazine while the airway is protected

🔍 Key Clues: 24-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — give the next dose of haloperidol as charted: Continuing the offending drug worsens the reaction

B — apply a collar and observe for an hour: A collar does not treat the cause and delay can allow airway obstruction

C — sedate him with a benzodiazepine and review later: Sedation alone does not reverse the dystonia and delays treatment

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: The reaction is recorded prominently so that the same drug is not restarted without cover
option_1: give the next dose of haloperidol as charted
option_2: apply a collar and observe for an hour
option_3: sedate him with a benzodiazepine and review later
option_4: stay with him, keep the airway safe, and give the prescribed intramuscular promethazine without delay

question: A patient on an antipsychotic paces up and down the ward and cannot remain seated, though he has no tremor or rigidity. This is:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. akathisia

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Akathisia is a subjective sense of inner restlessness with the compulsion to keep moving, and it often appears soon after the dose is raised

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — an exacerbation of psychosis: The picture is a drug effect and not a worsening of the illness

C — tardive dyskinesia: Tardive dyskinesia affects the face, lips and tongue with involuntary movements

D — catatonia: Catatonia produces immobility, stupor or waxy flexibility

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Akathisia is often mistaken for agitation and the dose is wrongly increased, which makes it worse and may lead to suicide

question: Which feature indicates drug induced parkinsonism rather than idiopathic Parkinson disease?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. the movements begin within weeks of starting the drug, are usually symmetrical and improve when the drug is stopped

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Drug induced parkinsonism appears soon after the drug is started or the dose increased, is generally symmetrical and settles when the drug is withdrawn

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — loss of the sense of smell: Loss of smell points to idiopathic Parkinson disease

B — asymmetry of the tremor at the beginning of the illness: Early asymmetry favours idiopathic Parkinson disease

D — a good response to levodopa from the outset: Drug induced parkinsonism responds to anticholinergics and only poorly to levodopa

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: The nurse records the time of onset of tremor and rigidity in relation to any change in the drug chart, as this is the clue to the cause
option_2: asymmetry of the tremor at the beginning of the illness
option_3: the movements begin within weeks of starting the drug, are usually symmetrical and improve when the drug is stopped
option_4: a good response to levodopa from the outset

question: Tardive dyskinesia is characterised by:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. involuntary repetitive movements of the tongue, lips and face appearing after months or years of antipsychotic treatment

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Tardive dyskinesia is a late onset syndrome of involuntary orofacial movements that may persist after the drug is stopped

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — a coarse tremor that disappears during sleep: A tremor that disappears in sleep is characteristic of Parkinson disease

B — sudden fever with rigidity and a raised creatine kinase: Fever with rigidity and a raised creatine kinase describes neuroleptic malignant syndrome

C — painful spasm of the eye muscles: Painful spasm of the eye muscles is acute oculogyric dystonia

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: The abnormal movements are assessed with a standard rating scale every few months so that the earliest signs are detected
option_1: a coarse tremor that disappears during sleep
option_2: sudden fever with rigidity and a raised creatine kinase
option_4: involuntary repetitive movements of the tongue, lips and face appearing after months or years of antipsychotic treatment

question: A 30-year-old man on haloperidol for four days develops a temperature of 39.8 degrees Celsius, generalised muscular rigidity and profuse sweating, and he is drowsy and unstable. The nurse should first:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. withhold the antipsychotic, start urgent cooling and monitoring and inform the psychiatrist at once

🧠 Clinical Rationale: This is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a life threatening reaction, so the drug is stopped at once and emergency supportive treatment is started

🔍 Key Clues: 30-year-old | 39.8 degrees Celsius

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — start oral fluids and review in the morning: Oral fluids do not treat a severe autonomic and muscular emergency

B — give the next dose to control the psychosis: Continuing the antipsychotic is dangerous

C — give paracetamol and continue the drug: Continuing the drug allows the reaction to progress and antipyretics alone are useless

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome carries a high mortality if it is not recognised early, so fever with rigidity in any patient on an antipsychotic is treated as an emergency
option_1: start oral fluids and review in the morning
option_2: give the next dose to control the psychosis
option_4: withhold the antipsychotic, start urgent cooling and monitoring and inform the psychiatrist at once

question: The accepted therapeutic serum level of lithium in the maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder is:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. 0.6 to 1.2 milliequivalents per litre

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A level of about 0.6 to 1.2 milliequivalents per litre controls the mood while staying below the toxic range

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 5 to 10 milliequivalents per litre: A level of 5 to 10 is far above the therapeutic range and would be fatal

C — 0.01 to 0.05 milliequivalents per litre: This range is far too low to have any effect

D — 20 to 30 milliequivalents per litre: This range is toxic and has no place in treatment

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Lithium is usually taken twice a day so that the level stays steady, and the sample is collected twelve hours after the last dose

question: A 42-year-old woman on lithium has had diarrhoea and vomiting for two days. She is now coarse and tremulous and unsteady on her feet. The most likely explanation is:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. lithium toxicity precipitated by dehydration

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Dehydration reduces renal lithium excretion and pushes the level into the toxic range, causing a coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion

🔍 Key Clues: 42-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — an acute dystonic reaction: Dystonic reactions occur with antipsychotics and not with lithium

C — alcohol withdrawal: Alcohol withdrawal produces tremor and sweating with a different history

D — a relapse of mania: A manic relapse does not cause ataxia of this kind

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Withhold the next dose, inform the doctor and arrange a lithium level at once, because toxicity can progress to seizures and renal failure

question: Which instruction is most important for a patient taking lithium?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. drink a normal amount of fluid and keep a steady salt intake, and avoid dehydration

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A steady salt and fluid intake keeps lithium excretion predictable, while dehydration or a low salt diet raises the level

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — take the drug only when the mood is low: Lithium is taken continuously to prevent relapse and not only in low mood

B — stop the drug as soon as the mood becomes normal: Stopping abruptly can trigger a relapse, so the drug is continued as prescribed

C — restrict all salt in the diet: A very low salt intake reduces lithium excretion and causes toxicity

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Patients are also warned about the risk of toxicity with diuretics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and some antihypertensives
option_1: take the drug only when the mood is low
option_2: stop the drug as soon as the mood becomes normal
option_4: drink a normal amount of fluid and keep a steady salt intake, and avoid dehydration

question: A patient started on clozapine must have a regular blood count because the drug can cause:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. agranulocytosis

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, so the white cell count is checked weekly for the first eighteen weeks and less often after that

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — polycythaemia: Polycythaemia is an increase in red cells and is not caused by clozapine

B — thrombocytosis: An increase in platelets is not the concern

C — haemolysis: Haemolysis is not the recognised hazard of clozapine

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Any fever or sore throat in a patient on clozapine must be reported at once, since it may be the first sign of a falling white cell count

question: A 28-year-old man on olanzapine for a year has gained 12 kg, his waist has increased and his fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL. The nurse's most appropriate action is to:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. record the weight, waist and glucose, and ask the team to review the drug while advising diet and exercise

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Atypicals cause weight gain and metabolic disturbance, so regular monitoring with diet and exercise advice and a team review of the drug is the correct plan

🔍 Key Clues: 28-year-old | 12 kg | 118 mg/dL

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — restrict his food intake severely without any plan: Severe unsupervised restriction risks poor nutrition and is not the recommended approach

C — stop the drug without telling the team: No nurse may stop a prescribed drug on her own

D — tell him that weight gain is not related to the drug: Denying the link destroys trust and prevents the patient from acting on it

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Weight, waist circumference, blood pressure and fasting glucose are recorded at least every six months in any patient on a long term antipsychotic
option_1: restrict his food intake severely without any plan
option_2: record the weight, waist and glucose, and ask the team to review the drug while advising diet and exercise
option_3: stop the drug without telling the team
option_4: tell him that weight gain is not related to the drug

question: A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia stops his tablets every time he feels better and has had three relapses in two years. The most useful step is to:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. discuss the pattern with him and the team so that a long acting depot preparation can be considered

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A depot preparation removes the need for daily tablets and is offered after discussing the pattern of relapse with the patient

🔍 Key Clues: 35-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — tell the family to hide the tablets: Concealing tablets damages trust and is not acceptable

C — increase the oral dose to twice the usual amount: Doubling the dose is outside the nurse's role and does not address the adherence problem

D — discharge him without treatment: Discharge without treatment leaves him at risk of another relapse

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Non-adherence is common because patients feel well and dislike side effects, so the reason for it is explored rather than blamed
option_1: tell the family to hide the tablets
option_2: discuss the pattern with him and the team so that a long acting depot preparation can be considered
option_3: increase the oral dose to twice the usual amount

question: Which is an example of an open ended question?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Tell me what has been on your mind since yesterday.

🧠 Clinical Rationale: An open ended question invites the patient to describe his experience in his own words and gives no fixed answer

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Were you scared?: This suggests the expected answer and is a leading closed question

B — Are you feeling better today?: This also invites only a yes or a no

D — Did you sleep well last night?: A question answerable with yes or no is closed

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Open ended questions bring out the information the patient thinks is important rather than what the nurse has already assumed
option_3: Tell me what has been on your mind since yesterday.

question: When a patient falls silent and begins to cry during an interview, the most therapeutic response is to:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. sit quietly with him and give him time to continue when he is ready

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Deliberate silence gives the patient time to feel and to organise his thoughts, and the nurse's calm presence conveys acceptance

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — fill the silence by asking about his job: Changing the subject avoids the painful feeling and blocks the patient

C — tell him to stop crying and be strong: This shames the patient and stops all further expression

D — leave the room immediately: Leaving the room abandons him at a vulnerable moment

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Silence is an active therapeutic technique, but it must be accompanied by an attentive posture and eye contact
option_1: sit quietly with him and give him time to continue when he is ready
option_2: fill the silence by asking about his job
option_3: tell him to stop crying and be strong

question: A 31-year-old woman with severe depression says she is worthless and that her family would be better off without her. The nurse replies, "You are not worthless at all, and your family loves you." This response is unsuitable because it:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. gives false reassurance and dismisses her feelings instead of exploring them

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Denying the patient's expressed feeling closes the conversation and prevents the nurse from assessing the risk behind her statement

🔍 Key Clues: 31-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — asks too many questions: No question is asked at all

B — makes use of silence: The reply is a statement and not an example of silence

C — is too long a reply: The length of the reply is not the problem

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: A statement such as being a burden to the family is a warning sign of suicide risk and must be explored, not contradicted
option_4: gives false reassurance and dismisses her feelings instead of exploring them

question: A 45-year-old man says, "I am frightened that I will lose my job because of this illness." Which reply best uses empathy?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. It sounds as though losing your job frightens you a great deal.

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Restating the feeling in the nurse's own words shows that the patient has been heard and invites him to say more

🔍 Key Clues: 45-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Many patients feel that way, so do not worry.: Comparing him with other patients minimises his personal fear

C — There is nothing to worry about, everything will be fine.: This is false reassurance and dismisses the worry

D — You should think about your health first and your job later.: This gives advice before the feeling has been explored

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Empathy means recognising and naming the feeling, not agreeing with the content of the fear
option_1: Many patients feel that way, so do not worry.
option_2: It sounds as though losing your job frightens you a great deal.
option_3: There is nothing to worry about, everything will be fine.
option_4: You should think about your health first and your job later.

question: Which is the main reason that a question beginning with the word "why" is avoided in a therapeutic interview?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. it tends to demand justification and makes the patient feel defensive or judged

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A why question asks the patient to justify his behaviour and often produces guilt, defensiveness or a superficial answer

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — it takes too long to answer: Length is not the reason

B — it is not understood by patients: The words are understood but the effect is the problem

D — it is grammatically incorrect: The construction is grammatical but therapeutically unhelpful

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Such questions are rephrased to begin with what or how, which invite description rather than defence
option_3: it tends to demand justification and makes the patient feel defensive or judged

question: A 26-year-old man is shouting and striking the wall but has not touched anyone. Before considering restraint the nurse should:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. use verbal de-escalation in a quiet area, offer choices and remove the audience

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The least restrictive measure comes first, so de-escalation with a quiet space, a calm voice and simple choices is tried before any restraint

🔍 Key Clues: 26-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — isolate him in a locked room without any order: Seclusion requires a medical order and cannot be started by the nurse alone

C — call the security staff at once: Calling security escalates the situation before other measures are tried

D — give an injection against his will: An involuntary injection without an order or a legal basis is assault

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Document both the behaviour and the de-escalation measures tried, as this record justifies any later use of restraint
option_1: use verbal de-escalation in a quiet area, offer choices and remove the audience
option_2: isolate him in a locked room without any order

question: A patient has been placed in seclusion for violent behaviour towards other patients with a written order. Which nursing action is essential?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. check on him every fifteen minutes and record his behaviour, physical state and the reason for continuing seclusion

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A patient in seclusion is observed at frequent and regular intervals, with the behaviour, physical condition and the continuing justification all recorded

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — give him his meals inside the seclusion room: Meals and toilet breaks come out of seclusion, as seclusion is by definition the isolation of the patient and not a punishment

C — review the order only after twenty four hours: The order must be reviewed much sooner, usually every few hours

D — leave him undisturbed so that he can calm down: Leaving him alone and unobserved is unsafe and defeats the monitoring requirement

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Seclusion is ended as soon as the risk falls, since prolonged isolation can itself cause harm
option_1: give him his meals inside the seclusion room
option_2: check on him every fifteen minutes and record his behaviour, physical state and the reason for continuing seclusion
option_3: review the order only after twenty four hours
option_4: leave him undisturbed so that he can calm down

question: The principle of the least restrictive alternative in psychiatric care means that the nurse should:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. choose the measure that restricts the patient's freedom as little as possible while keeping everyone safe

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Care is planned so that safety is achieved with the smallest possible loss of freedom and dignity

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — keep the patient in hospital for as long as possible: Length of stay is decided by the clinical need and not by the principle

B — avoid all forms of treatment: Avoiding all treatment is not the intent, as safety is still required

D — use the strongest available measure first: The strongest measure is reserved for when lesser measures have failed

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: The same principle supports treating patients in the community wherever it is safe to do so
option_1: keep the patient in hospital for as long as possible
option_3: choose the measure that restricts the patient's freedom as little as possible while keeping everyone safe

question: A patient has been restrained on a bed for forty minutes. During the safety checks the nurse must particularly watch for:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. impaired circulation, breathing difficulty, skin damage and aspiration

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Restricted movement, pressure on the chest and an immobilised position put the patient at risk of impaired circulation, asphyxia, pressure injury and aspiration

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — a rise in appetite: Appetite is not affected by restraint

B — the patient's request for a newspaper: Reading material does not affect physical safety

C — complaints about the food: Food complaints are not the safety concern during restraint

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Restraint is never applied in the prone position, because the weight of others on the back has caused deaths from asphyxia
option_4: impaired circulation, breathing difficulty, skin damage and aspiration

question: Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, admission of a person as an independent patient is based on:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. his own free and informed consent

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Every person, including a person with mental illness, is presumed to have capacity, and admission is ordinarily on his own informed consent as an independent patient

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — an order of the police alone: A police order is not the basis of an independent admission

B — a certificate from a neighbour: A neighbour has no role in the admission process

D — the consent of his relatives alone: Relatives cannot consent on behalf of an adult who has capacity

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Where capacity is lacking, the law lays down a separate supported or involuntary admission process with an independent review

question: A 17-year-old girl with severe depression needs electroconvulsive therapy. Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 the correct position is that:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. electroconvulsive therapy may be given to a minor only with the informed consent of the guardian and with the approval of the concerned board

🧠 Clinical Rationale: For a minor the Act requires the informed consent of the guardian together with the approval of the concerned review board before electroconvulsive therapy is given

🔍 Key Clues: 17-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — electroconvulsive therapy is prohibited in minors in all situations: It is not an absolute prohibition, as a defined process exists

C — electroconvulsive therapy may be given freely to minors: The Act places restrictions and does not permit free use in minors

D — only the nurse's consent is required: The nurse's consent has no legal standing for such a procedure

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Emergency treatment to save a life is given first, but the board approval and the guardian's consent are documented without delay
option_1: electroconvulsive therapy is prohibited in minors in all situations
option_2: electroconvulsive therapy may be given to a minor only with the informed consent of the guardian and with the approval of the concerned board
option_3: electroconvulsive therapy may be given freely to minors

question: A 38-year-old woman with schizophrenia says the staff are plotting to poison her food, a belief she has held for two weeks. Which response is most therapeutic?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. You feel that the staff want to harm you; the food here is safe and I will eat with you.

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The nurse acknowledges the feeling without confirming the false belief and offers a concrete action that reduces fear

🔍 Key Clues: 38-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Let us not talk about the food today.: Changing the subject leaves the fear unaddressed

C — Nobody here would ever poison you; that is impossible.: A flat denial tempts the patient to argue and does not reduce the fear

D — You must stop saying such things about the staff.: This sounds like a reprimand and damages trust

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Beliefs are neither agreed with nor argued about, and the conversation is gently moved to the here and now
option_1: You feel that the staff want to harm you; the food here is safe and I will eat with you.
option_2: Let us not talk about the food today.
option_3: Nobody here would ever poison you; that is impossible.
option_4: You must stop saying such things about the staff.

question: Which of the following is a barrier to effective communication?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. the use of technical jargon that the patient does not understand

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Technical terms that the listener cannot interpret block understanding and make the message meaningless

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — maintaining eye contact at a comfortable level: Comfortable eye contact supports communication

C — listening attentively to the patient: Attentive listening is a facilitator rather than a barrier

D — using simple and clear language: Simple clear language improves communication

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Instructions should be given in the patient's own language, as jargon and unfamiliar English words are a common cause of misunderstanding
option_1: maintaining eye contact at a comfortable level
option_2: the use of technical jargon that the patient does not understand

question: Reading a book while music plays in the background shows:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. divided attention

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Divided attention is the sharing of attention between two tasks or stimuli at the same time

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — a disorder of perception: No disorder of perception is shown

C — inattention: Inattention means a failure to attend, which is not the case here

D — fluctuation of attention: Fluctuation of attention is the shifting of attention from one object to another over time

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Concentration is poor in anxiety and depression, so the nurse gives short instructions and checks understanding

question: Forgetting because newly learnt material interferes with the recall of older material is called:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. retroactive interference

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Retroactive interference is the disruptive effect of new learning on the recall of what was learnt earlier

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — repression: Repression is the unconscious pushing out of painful memories

C — proactive interference: Proactive interference is the opposite, where earlier learning interferes with new material

D — amnesia: Amnesia is a loss of memory from injury or disease rather than from interference

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: New information taught just after other material is easily lost, so teaching is spaced and repeated

question: The theory of emotion which states that bodily changes come first and the emotion follows the perception of those changes is:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. the James-Lange theory

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The James-Lange theory holds that the physiological reaction occurs first and the subjective feeling follows from it

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — the Cannon-Bard theory: The Cannon-Bard theory says that the body change and the emotional experience occur together

C — the two factor theory of Schachter and Singer: The two factor theory adds a cognitive label to the physiological arousal

D — the cognitive appraisal theory: Cognitive appraisal theory emphasises the interpretation of the situation

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Understanding this helps the nurse explain to a patient why the racing heart of anxiety can itself increase the feeling of fear
option_3: the two factor theory of Schachter and Singer

question: The theory of multiple intelligences, which includes musical and bodily-kinaesthetic abilities, was proposed by:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Howard Gardner

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Gardner proposed that intelligence is not a single general ability but a set of relatively independent intelligences

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Charles Spearman: Spearman proposed a single general factor called g

C — Alfred Binet: Binet developed one of the first practical intelligence tests
